Micro-aeration for hydrogen sulfide reduction in full-scale anaerobic 
digesters with limited headspace: Performance and sulfide 
reduction kinetics
Ali Khadir a
, George Nakhla a
, Renisha Karki b
, Lutgarde Raskin b
, Christopher Muller c,  
Karla Guevarra d, Amanda Summers d, Laurie Pierce d, Parisa Shahbaz d
, Kati Bell c,  
Steven Skerlos b, Embrey Bronstad c,*
a Department of Chemical and Biochemical Engineering, Thompson Engineering Building, Western University, London, Ontario, Canada
b Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI, United States,
c Brown and Caldwell, 1527 Cole Blvd #300, Lakewood, CO 80401, United States
d Pierce County Planning and Public Works - Sewer Division, 9850 64th St. W, University Place, WA, United States
A R T I C L E  I N F O
Keywords:
Micro-aeration
Hydrogen sulfide
Sulfide oxidizing microbes
Anaerobic digestion
Desulfurization kinetics
A B S T R A C T
A full-scale trial of micro-aeration was conducted at a municipal wastewater plant using two anaerobic digesters 
with limited headspace, one as a control and one as a test. A reduction of approximately 13 %–16 % in hydrogen 
sulfide biogas concentrations was observed in the test digester. Microbial community analyses were also con­
ducted at steady-state conditions to determine differences between the microbial ecology of the test and the 
control digesters. Although sulfide removal typically occurs in the headspace of a micro-aerated digester, the 
data generated by this pilot study developed a new approach to quantify the contribution of liquid phase sulfide 
oxidizing microbes (SOM).
1. Introduction
Hydrogen sulfide (H2S) is a common constituent of biogas produced 
during the anaerobic digestion (AD) of municipal wastewater sludge, 
and its concentration in biogas is dictated primarily by the sulfur content 
of the AD feed. Peu et al. (2012) reported H2S concentrations in biogas 
as high as 19,000 parts per million (ppm). However, H2S in municipal 
AD biogas typically averages 50–5000 ppm (Dumont, 2015). The pres­
ence of H2S creates corrosive condensates that reduce the operational 
life of gas handling systems and damage gas pipelines and engines that 
receive the biogas in beneficial end-use projects.
Traditional biogas desulfurization techniques, such as granular 
activated carbon or wet scrubbing systems that use water or chemicals, 
require media replacement and disposal of the spent media. Micro- 
aeration, or the introduction of small quantities of air or oxygen into 
anaerobic digesters to facilitate the biological oxidation of sulfide by 
sulfide oxidizing microorganisms (SOM), is a promising, simple and 
economical biogas desulfurization technology (Fdz.-Polanco et al., 
2009; Jeníˇcek et al., 2017; Krayzelova et al., 2014; Nguyen and Khanal, 
2018; Ramos et al., 2013). It has been successfully applied at full-scale 
municipal wastewater treatment plants with H2S concentrations of 
500–5000 ppm resulting in H2S removal efficiencies of 85–99.5 % 
(Jeníˇcek et al., 2017). Romero et al. (2020) presented results from three 
mesophilic full-scale micro-aeration applications, two in the US and one 
in Australia. The two anaerobic digesters in the US produced biogas at 
4500–5000 m3/d, with average H2S concentrations of 1125–5000 ppm. 
Micro-aeration was applied by injecting air into the sludge recirculation 
lines, which achieved about 80 % reduction of H2S. The Australian plant 
applied micro-aeration in the liquid phase to a mesophilic anaerobic 
digester with a relatively low biogas H2S concentration of about 
600 ppm. The micro-aeration performance for this system was unstable, 
with removal efficiencies averaging 40 %, occasionally reaching 90 %.
Most literature on the role of biogas residence time (RT) in biogas 
desulfurization was based on directly injecting air into the headspace of 
pilot units with biogas RTs of 1.4–8 h (Ramos et al., 2014; Kobayashi 
et al., 2012; Khoshnevisan et al., 2017). Removal efficiencies of 
68 %–> 99 % were reported at these RTs; moreover, biogas RTs of five 
hours or more resulted in approximately 90 % removal efficiencies

(Khoshnevisan et al., 2017). Ramos et al. (2014) evaluated the impact of 
micro-aeration in pilot scale digesters at a biogas RT of 6.8–8.6 h, which 
resulted in 97 %–100 % H2S reduction. A full-scale study also evaluated 
air addition into the headspace of a mesophilic digester treating dairy 
cow manure (Kobayashi et al., 2012). At a biogas RT of 1.35–1.7 h and 
air addition at 1 % (v/v) of the biogas, the study achieved an average of 
68 % H2S removal efficiency for H2S biogas concentrations of 
2000–4000 ppm. Using biogas RTs reported by Khoshnevisan et al. 
(2017), Muller et al. (2022) established a first-order rate constant for 
H2S removal in the range of 0.52 h−1. However, data from full-scale 
plants on the impact of biogas RT with liquid phase injection of air/­
oxygen are lacking and no information is available for digesters with 
limited headspace.
Not only is full-scale experience for digesters with limited headspace 
lacking, a recent review by Muller et al. (2022) also identified the need 
for better descriptions of SOM kinetics in the liquid phase. The available

kinetic data from lab studies (Andreides et al., 2021; Nielsen and Vol­
lertsen, 2021; Pokorna-Krayzelova, 2017) are derived from experi­
mental designs using high dissolved oxygen concentrations that are not 
reflective of real-world conditions. Further exploration of SOM kinetics 
would better enable the delineation and quantification of liquid vs. gas 
phase desulfurization. This would enable the development of more ac­
curate sulfur and COD mass balances as well as improved AD models.
Micro-aeration has potential as an economical biogas de- 
sulfurization method, but there are knowledge gaps regarding SOM ki­
netics and the effects of micro-aeration on AD performance metrics and 
the microbial community. There are inconsistent reports on improve­
ments to AD performance metrics due to micro-aeration. Despite re­
ported improvement in hydrolysis rates (Nguyen and Khanal, 2018), 
stabilization of volatile fatty acid (VFA) accumulation, and indications 
that the transformation of lactic, valeric, butyric, and propionic acids to 
acetate is enhanced in the presence of oxygen (Lim and Wang, 2013), the 
impact of micro-aeration on volatile solids reduction (VSR) and methane 
yield is contradictory. Jenicek et al. (2017) noted a 1.6 %–9.3 % 
decrease in the overall sludge volatile fraction with micro-aeration and 
average increases in biogas and methane production of 17 % and 16 %, 
respectively. In contrast, Diak et al. observed that micro-aeration of 
municipal primary sludge had no effect on the degradation of carbo­
hydrates and VS reduction even though it enhanced the generation of 
soluble proteins and ammonia (Diak et al., 2013).
The objective of this study was to evaluate the biogas desulfurization 
efficiency at very short biogas RT, with air injection into the liquid 
rather than the headspace. To evaluate the efficacy of adopting micro- 
aeration in digesters with limited headspace, the study further 
assessed the contribution of liquid phase biological sulfide oxidation to 
the overall desulfurization. Sulfur mass balances were developed to 
assess the impact of micro-aeration on key performance indicators. 
Finally, the microbial community structures in micro-aerated and con­
ventional digesters were compared to evaluate if micro-aeration resulted 
in greater SOM abundance.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Evaluation of the impact of micro-aeration on desulfurization in pilot 
study
2.1.1. Plant description
The study was conducted at a wastewater treatment facility with an 
average dry weather flow capacity of 45 million gallons per day (mgd) 
(204,574 m3/day); Fig. 1a shows the overall process flow diagram while 
Fig. 1b shows the schematic of the pilot setup. The ratio of particulate 
COD (pCOD): volatile suspended solids (VSS) in the co-thickened pri­
mary sludge and waste activated sludge were 1.36 and 1.62, 
respectively.
2.1.2. Micro-aeration setup and baseline operation
Two circular waffle-bottom anaerobic digesters, each 27 m in 
diameter, were used for this study: one as a control (D4) and one as the 
test digester (D5). Each digester has a working volume of 6965 m3, a 
side water depth of approximately 12 m, and are mixed with draft tube 
mixing systems. The digesters are also equipped with submerged fixed 
covers that create a headspace volume of approximately 52 m3, result­
ing in a biogas retention time of approximately15 min The micro- 
aeration study was divided into two phases: Phase 1: Baseline Opera­
tions, and Phase 2: Full-Scale Implementation. Phase 1 established a 
baseline of characterization for biogas and digestate without the addi­
tion of air. Biogas flow, influent sludge flow, and digestate flow rates 
were monitored continuously. Biogas composition was measured twice a 
day and pH was measured daily. Feed and digestate total and volatile 
solids were measured twice a week. Digestate alkalinity and volatile 
fatty acids (VFA) were measured twice a week.
During Phase 2, the existing plant service air system was used to 
supply air to the sludge recirculation line upstream of the test digester, 
through a ½” line with air flow meters with needle valves, capable of 
regulating airflow in the range of 20–200 cfh (0.6–5.7 m3/h). Initial 
airflow rates were set at 90 scfh (2.5 m3/h) for 49 days to ensure that 
oxygen levels in the gas did not exceed 0.2 %. Subsequently, airflow 
rates were doubled to 180 scfh (5 m3/h) for 28 days and gas oxygen 
levels increased to the detection level of the gas meter. Then, the airflow 
rate was dropped to 140 scfh (3.9 m3/h) for the remainder of the study 
(180 days). Since the RT in both digesters is about 40 days, only the 
samples corresponding to the operation at 3.9 m3/h were analyzed for 
different chemical and microbial analyses as it spans more than three 
turnovers of the mean RT.
2.2. Offline batch test setup to evaluate SOM kinetics
Sulfur removal was investigated in two digestate samples taken from 
the control and test digesters a week before the termination of the 
microaeration trial. The digestate samples were subjected to air and N2 
injection to determine the biotic and abiotic (stripping) losses of dis­
solved sulfides, respectively. Once abiotic losses were determined, the 
rate of biological and chemical sulfide oxidation could be determined 
from the difference in rates between air and N2 injections.
The experiments were conducted in two reactors, each with a volume 
of 1.7 L (12 cm internal diameter and 15.5 cm high), which were filled 
with 1.4 L digestate at 35 ℃. Both N2 and air were injected to the reactor 
using a syringe pump (KD Scientific Inc., Holliston, Massachusetts, USA 
– LEGATO 100 Infuse Single model pump) equipped with a 5 mL 
Hamilton syringe and at a flow rate of 12 µL/min. This corresponds to a 
volumetric rate of 0.514 mL gas/L-h for 4 h, consistent with the full- 
scale micro-aeration rate of 3.9 m3/h in the 6965 m3 digester. While 
the digestate was introduced into the test reactor, N2 gas at a flowrate of 
0.3 m3/h was injected for 4 min to purge the reactor of air and avoid 
sulfur oxidation during filling. The offgas was collected in a 1 L canister 
with an initial vacuum pressure of −28.7 inHg for final gas analysis. At 
the end of the experiment, the offgas was sent to a commercial labora­
tory (ALS Environmental Labs, London, ON) for measurement of H2S. At 
time intervals 0, 30, 60, 90, 120, 180, and 240 min, samples were taken 
and measured for dissolved sulfide, sCOD, and VFA concentrations.
To assess the chemical oxidation of hydrogen sulfide, tests with 30 % 
hydrogen peroxide (H2O2—density 1.13 g/mL, 0.16 g O2/mL) dosed at 
100 times the rate of oxygen were also performed. Thus, to avoid oxygen 
limiting conditions, 30 % H2O2 was injected at a flowrate of 2.08 µL/ 
min resulting in an injection of 100 times more oxygen with peroxide 
compared to air (0.33 mg O2/min vs 0.0033 mg O2/min).
2.3. Chemical analyses
Daily biogas production was measured in real time by the waste­
water plant and composition wea measured using a BIOGAS 5000 m 
(Landtec QED, Dexter MI) throughout the pilot study. The digestate 
samples were tested for total sulfur (EPA 6010D, 2018), dissolved sulfur 
(Martin et al., 1994), and dissolved sulfates (EPA 375.2, 1993). The 
sCOD, VFA concentrations were analyzed using HACH methods (HACH, 
Loveland, Colorado). The total solids (Method 2540A), total suspended 
solids (Method 2540D), volatile solids (Method 2540B), and volatile 
suspended solids (Method 2540E) were analyzed following standard 
methods (American Public Health Association, 2023).
For offline batch test, the dissolved sulfide concentration was 
measured using HACH method (HACH, Loveland, Colorado). Sulfide 
TNT vials had a range of 0.1–2.0 mg S2-/L, and therefore samples were 
diluted with deionized water prior to measurement.
2.4. Microbial analyses
Digestate samples from micro-aeration pilot study were shipped 
overnight on ice to the University of Michigan for microbial analyses.

Upon arrival, samples were centrifuged at 10,000 g for 10 min at 4 ◦C, 
the supernatants were decanted, and biomass pellets were stored at −80 
℃ until DNA extraction. DNA extraction was performed using DNeasy 
PowerSoil Pro Kit (QIAGEN, Venlo, The Netherlands) following the 
manufacturer’s instructions with minor modifications, which included 
bead beating (Mini-Beadbeater-96, BioSpec Products, Bartlesville, OK, 
USA) three times for 2 min each using Lysing Matrix E tubes. DNA 
quality and quantity were determined via spectrophotometry (Nano­
drop 1000, Thermo Fisher Scientific, Wilmington, DE, USA) and Qubit 
2.0 Fluorometer (Invitrogen, Life Technologies, CA, USA). The DNA 
extracts were then submitted to the Host Microbiome Initiative (Uni­
versity of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI, USA) for 16S rRNA gene sequencing 
via Illumina MiSeq (San Diego, CA, USA). Universal primers F515 and 
R806 targeting the V4 region of the 16S rRNA gene (Caporoso et al., 
2011) were used for PCR amplification. The raw sequence data were 
submitted to NCBI under accession number PRJNA1149829. The se­
quences obtained were processed using DADA2 v.1.26 (Callahan et al., 
2016).

2.5. Statistical analyses
The statistical analyses were conducted using Excel data tools 
packages. The t-tests were conducted at a 95 % confidence interval.
3. Results and discussion
3.1. Impact of micro-aeration on desulfurization
3.1.1. Overall performance of control and test digesters
Table 1 lists the overall averages and standard deviations of the main 
operational parameters for the control and test digesters during the 
baseline and micro-aeration at 3.9 m3/h. The feed total solids concen­
tration averaged 8.2 % (82 gTS/L) and the volatile solids averaged 
7.31 % (73 gVS/L), representing an average volatile fraction of 89.2 %. 
The volatile fraction of raw primary sludge and WAS were 95 % and 
84 %, respectively, while the ratio of particulate COD to VSS in the 
primary sludge and WAS were 1.36 and 1.62, respectively. Primary 
sludge accounted for 62.5 % of the combined primary sludge and WAS 
VS loading, as compared with 58 % during the micro-aeration study. 
The plant recycles digested sludge to ensure pumpability of the influent 
thickened combined sludge at 8.2 % solids, therefore the volatile solids 
reduction (VSR) efficiencies have been calculated on the basis of the 
influent primary and WAS solids listed in Table 1. It should be noted that 
despite the atypically high volatile fraction (76 % of the digested 
sludge), the VSR based on the influent average VS mass during the 
baseline study was about 54 %. The relatively high volatile fraction of 
the digestate is indicative of high influent non-biodegradable VSS, 
potentially from a fiber board manufacturing plant. During micro- 
aeration, VSR was 54.3 %, almost identical to the baseline condition, 
despite slightly higher influent flows.
Figs. 2a and 2b illustrate the temporal variation of biogas flow and 
specific methane yield (SMY in m3/kg VS). It is evident that both biogas 
and SMY remained relatively stable during both the baseline study and 
the test period. The performance stability is corroborated by the low 
relative standard deviations of the various parameters depicted in 
Table 1. Using the aforementioned pCOD:VSS ratio of 1.62 for WAS and 
1.36 for primary sludge, for the baseline study, the observed SMY 
theoretically corresponds to about 66 % VSR, which is greater than the 
observed VSR. However, during the micro-aeration study, the observed 
SMY reflects 57.7 % VSR, in close agreement with the 54.3 % reported 
above on VS mass basis.
3.1.2. Impact of micro-aeration on sulfide concentrations
Figs. 3a and 3b show the temporal variations of H2S concentrations, 
and mass flows, respectively, while Fig. 3c shows the H2S removal ef­
ficiency based on differences in concentrations and mass rates. It is 
evident from Fig. 3a that during the baseline study, there were no sta­
tistically significant differences in gaseous H2S concentrations, with 
both digesters averaging about 2100 ppm. H2S concentrations dropped 
by 20 % to about 1700 ppm in both digesters at the onset of the micro- 
aeration. It should be noted that as shown in Fig. 3b, even during the 
baseline study, the H2S mass rate in the test digester were lower than the 
control due to the roughly 5 % lower gas production (Table 1) resulting 
from the slightly lower feed flow. The removal efficiencies in Fig. 3c 
clearly indicate that the H2S concentrations in the biogas from the two 
digesters started to diverge with the initiation of micro-aeration. The 
average H2S concentration in the test digester of 1470 ppm was 13 % 
lower than the control. On a mass basis, due to an 8 % lower biogas on 
average in the test digester relative to the control digester, the percent 
reduction in H2S mass was 20 %.
. The differences between the control and test digester with respect to 
SMY (p = 0.0997), and methane production/mass of VS reduced 
(p = 0.198), were insignificant. Differences in digester VFA were sta­
tistically significant (p = 0.0035) with test digester averaging about 
10 % higher VFA concentrations. The 13 % decrease in biogas H2S be­
tween the test and the control digester discussed above was statistically 
significant (p = 1.84E-69). The difference between the control digester 
average methane content of 57 %, and 56 % in the control and test di­
gesters was statistically significant (p = 1.37E-12).

Oxygen in the control digester biogas was negligible but averaged 
0.5 %+ 0.01 % in the test digester. Using the correlation between % O2 
concentration in the biogas reported by Muller et al. (2022) being equal 
to 0.22 x volumetric percentage of airflow/biogas flow, the estimated 
average oxygen in the test digester biogas is 0.4 %, in close agreement 
with the observed average. The mass ratio of oxygen supplied: H2S 
removed was 10.8+ 3.1, much higher than the stoichiometric require­
ment of 0.5 kg O2/kg S. Giordano et al. reported that in full-scale sys­
tems with micro-aeration applied to the digester headspace, typically 
the air supplied should be 4 times the theoretical requirements 
(Giordano, et al., 2019). The considerable increase in demand above 
theoretical requirements is attributable to myriad other processes in the 
digester (facultative organisms scavenging dissolved oxygen, for 
example) which can consume up to 59 % of the oxygen supplied. 
Although delineating the oxygen transfer efficiency in the test digester 
was beyond the scope of this work, considering the 12 m-deep digester, 
oxygen transfer efficiency to the liquid is expected to be very high, thus 
resulting in low oxygen in the digester headspace, rationalizing the high 
O2: H2S ratio.
It should be noted that based on the VSR reduction efficiencies of 
about 54 %, the SMY should be around 0.36–0.38 m3/kg VS in, as 
indicated by the averages reported in Table 2, and thus values above that 
range are not realistic and only reflective of the heterogeneity of the feed 
and lack of representativeness of the grab sampling approach used. 
Figs. 4a and 4b show a downward slope of the SMY with gaseous H2S 
concentrations in the range of 1000–1500 ppm, suggesting potential 
inhibition due to H2S. Similarly, within the observed SMY range, the 
SMY appears to increase with decreasing VFAs. Sulfide toxicity to 
methanogens have been reported to follow a non-competitive inhibition 
model (Paula Jr. and Foresti, 2009) which is the default inhibition 
model in ADM1 (Barrera et al., 2015). The inhibition constant (KI), 
corresponding to 50 % inhibition has been reported to vary from 10 mg

(Metcalf et al., 2013), and a thus a gaseous concentration of 1 ppm

Thus, 1 mg/L of dissolved H2S is equivalent to 373 ppm. At the pH of 7.3 
at 37 ◦C, the pKa1 for H2S is 6.75 (Migidisov et al., 2002), and thus the 
unionized fraction of dissolved sulfides is 22 %. Hence, the gaseous H2S 
concentrations of about 1500 ppm would correspond to 0.88 mg 
H2S-S/L, and thus the reduction in specific methane yield 
(1-(KI/(KI+S)), based on the two extremes of KI would range from 0.3 % 
to 8 % only. It should be noted that the relative standard deviation of the 
SMY reported in Table 1 is about 16 %, which would mask the reported 
SMY reduction.
3.1.3. Evaluation of sulfur species
Muller et al. (2022) identified the lack of reliable sulfur mass bal­
ances, both in full-scale and pilot-scale applications. For plants that use 
iron to precipitate phosphorous, the sulfur content of digestate on dry 
mass basis is typically higher than the raw sludge (Dewil et al., 2009), 
which combined with the difficulty of quantifying sulfur precipitated in 
biogas headspace and piping, makes the closure of the sulfur mass bal­
ance very challenging. Dewil et al. assessed the fate of sulfur in four 
full-scale wastewater treatment plants in Belgium and observed that 
sulfur concentrations in biosolids (as a percent of dry solids) increased 
significantly after digestion at facilities that use iron to precipitate 
phosphorous, as iron bound to the released sulfides. For plants that do 
not use iron, there was essentially no change in sulfur content after 
digestion.
The facility at which this study was conducted does not add iron for 
phosphorus recovery. Seven samples from each of the two digesters 
(control-D4, and test-D5) were collected at the end of the micro-aeration 
study, the longest steady state operating period, and analyzed for total 
sulfur. The sulfur content as a percent of total solids averaged 0.86 %+
0.12 % in D5 and 0.95 %+ 0.29 % in D4. Similarly, the average total 
dissolved sulfur in D4 and D5 were 64+ 40, and 57+ 59 mgS/L, 
respectively. The average dissolved sulfides in D4 and D5 were 
11.6+ 10.3, and 9.7+ 11 mgS/L, respectively. Table 2 presents the 
sulfur mass balance to the digesters based on the average parameters 
reported in Table 1, with a mass balance closure of 77 % for the diges­
tion system. At the pH of 7.3 at 37 ◦C, the pKa1 for H2S is 6.75 (Migidisov 
et al., 2002). An absence of sulfates in the reduced anaerobic environ­
ment means the 22 % un-ionized fraction of dissolved sulfides corre­
sponds to 2.4 and 2.7 kg/d, in the control and test digesters, 
respectively. Therefore, in the control digester, the gas phase H2S mass 
rate was 5.5 times that in the liquid phase, as compared to four-fold in 
the test digester. This clearly attests to the significant effect of stripping 
and volatilization of H2S from the liquid, implying that effective bio­
logical desulfurization predominantly needs to occur in the gas phase. 
Furthermore, given the slow kinetics of SOM in the liquid phase under 
micro-aerobic conditions, as discussed later, the effect of liquid phase 
biological oxidation is bound to be of limited efficacy. The precipitation 
of H2S to sulfur in the liquid phase should result in a proportional in­
crease in the sulfur content of digestate. However, the total sulfur, as a 
percent of total solids, in the test digestate was lower than the control 
despite similar total solids (Table 1), which indicates that the sulfur 
precipitation appears to have occurred predominantly in the headspace. 
The 23 % discrepancy between the effluent and influent total sulfur 
mass rates could be due to a combination of factors, such as loss of H2S in 
feed and recirculation pumps, sulfur deposited on the digester walls, 
cover and gas pipes (as shown in SI Figure SI-3), as well as variations in 
raw sludge quality. Paing et al. conducted a detailed evaluation of an 
anerobic lagoon over a one-year period to both estimate H2S emissions 
and develop the sulfur mass balance, and concluded that despite the 
extensive sampling and monitoring, about 30 % of the influent total 
sulfur could not be accounted for (Paing, et al., 2003). Ruan et al. 
studied the speciation of various forms of sulfur in lab-scale micro-a­
erated anaerobic digesters loaded with scrap iron for H2S control and 
accounted not only for soluble and particulate sulfur but also sulfur 
precipitated on the digester walls, reported a sulfur mass balance closure 
of 90 %, with sulfur deposits on the digester walls contributing about 
20 % to the sulfur mass in the system (Ruan et al., 2017). The variability 
of sulfur emissions from various unit processes was demonstrated by 
Forouzanmehr et al. during a two-week sampling campaign of a 620,000 
population equivalent IFAS-based wastewater treatment plant in South 
France. The study reported that while the relative standard deviation of 
sulfur mass rates in sludges and liquids was mostly around 20 %, it 
increased to 50 % in gaseous emissions (Forouzanmehr, et al., 2021).
3.1.4. Impact of micro-aeration on microbial communities
The dominant amplicon sequence variants (ASVs) present at a rela­
tive abundance higher than 2 % in the two digesters were related to the 
genera Treponema, Smithella, Rikenellaceae RC9 gut group, Fastidiosipila, 
Blvii28 wastewater-sludge group (Acetobacteroides) (Fig. 5). Furthermore, 
Methanolinea and Methanothrix were the most abundant hydro­
genotrophic methanogenic and acetoclastic methanogenic genera, 
respectively.
As discussed above and elaborated upon later, no H2S removal was 
observed by the biomass in the liquid phase of the digesters, suggesting 
that the contribution of SOM in the digestate to the overall H2S removal 
was insignificant. Consistent with this, no known SOM genera were 
observed to be present at a relative abundance higher than 2 % by the 
16S rRNA gene analysis of the biomass samples obtained from the 
digestate. The SOM belonging to the genera Acidithiobacillus, Acineto­
bacter, Rhodococcus, Arcobacter, Sulfuricurvum, Halothiobacillus, Sulfur­
imonas, Thiomonas, are typically found in anaerobic bioreactorss 
subjected to micro-aeration. While there are a few studies that analyzed 
sulfide oxidation in the bulk solution, validation of sulfide oxidation 
based on the microbial communities was limiting (de Arespacochaga 
et al., 2014), as the relative abundances of SOM are very low. A 
micro-aeration study on lab-scale digesters treating chicken manure 
with a 40 d SRT achieved a 99.7 % reduction in biogas H2S through air 
injection into the liquid phase, with SOB (Sulfuricurvum, Thiobacillus, 
Acinetobacter, and Psedomonas) present at low relative abundances 
(0.1 %–0.6 %) in (Song et al., 2020). Similarly, in this study, Acineto­
bacter, Arcobacter, and Pseudomonas were observed at low relative 
abundances ranging from 0.03 % to 0.25 %. While oxygen affinity co­
efficients of the SOM have been observed lower than the air flow rates of 
this study, the microbial analysis and physicochemical tests suggest that 
there might be a possibility that the air supplied to the reactor was not 
utilized by the microorganisms in the liquid and escaped back to the 
headspace due to poor mixing conditions.
3.2. Kinetics of liquid-phase desulfurization in offline batch tests
The main objective of the offline batch testing was to assess the 
feasibility of biological sulfide oxidation with micro-aeration, under 
limiting dissolved oxygen conditions (below detection limits). The other 
objective was to assess whether micro-aeration improved hydrolysis and 
acidification in the digestate.

3.2.1. Sulfide oxidation in batch tests
Air, nitrogen, and hydrogen peroxide were introduced into the 1.4 L 
reactor that contained control digester sludge at rates of 12,12, and 
2.8 µL/min, respectively over a course of 4 hours.
Figs. 6a and 6b illustrate the effect of different gas injections on the 
total dissolved sulfides over time in the lab control and test digesters, 
respectively. The initial sulfide concentration of 25 mg/L decreased 
linearly to 15 mg/L by the end of the test using air as the aeration

medium. Similar trend was observed with N2 injections where the initial 
sulfide concentrations of 24 mg/L decreased to 16 mg/L over 4 hours. 
As evident from Fig. 5, under both micro-aeration with air or N2, the 
dissolved sulfides decreased linearly following zero-order kinetics, with 
specific rates of 0.042, and 0.039 mg/L-min. Using H2O2 at 100 times 
the oxygen flow rate (as air), the rate increased by 33 % to 0.0565 mg/L- 
min. In summary, using sludge from the full-scale control digester, total 
dissolved sulfide reductions of 40 %, 34 %, and 61 % were realized for 
air, N2, and H2O2 dosing, respectively.
The same pattern was also observed for batch tests using digested 
sludge from D5, the full-scale test digester. As illustrated in Fig. 6b, with 
air, initial sulfide concentrations decreased linearly from 21 mg/L to 
11 mg/L after 4 hrs; similar results were seen with N2 introduction 
where sulfide levels dropped from 16 mg/L to 9 mg/L, corresponding to 
rates of 0.035 and 0.029 mg/L-min, respectively. The rate with H2O2 
increased by 31 % to 0.046 mg/L-min. These align with the results from 
the batch tests using control digester. It is worth noting that the total 
amount of oxygen injected over the 4-hr test would stoichiometrically 
result in oxidation of maximum of 0.92 mg S/L.
Interestingly, sparging with air in both batch tests removed an in­
cremental 3 mgS/L relative to N2, which indicates that neither chemical 
nor biological sulfide oxidation but rather stripping accounted for the 
increased removal of sulfides with air. Using the typical H2O2 dose 
required to oxidize sulfides to sulfur of 2.4 mg H2O2/mgS (Fernando and 
Peters, 1988), the H2O2 added during the 4-hr test would theoretically 
oxidize 41 mgS/L, however, incremental sulfide removal with H2O2 
relative to N2 was 6 mgS/L in both batch studies. Considering the strong 
oxidation potential of organics with H2O2, it could be assumed that most 
of the peroxide was not used for sulfide oxidation. However, this 
assumption cannot be verified due to the lack of relevant data.
Buisman et al. who examined chemical oxidation of H2S levels of 
5–319 mg/L using dissolved oxygen concentrations of 0.1–8.5 mg/L 
determined that the rate of oxidation can be described by H2S0.41 ×
O20.39 (Buisman, et al., 1990). Given that dissolved oxygen concentra­
tions during the offline batch tests are expected to be very close in the 
two systems, the rate of H2S chemical oxidation would be proportional 
to H2S concentration. As evident from Figs. 6a and 6b, average dissolved 
sulfide concentrations during the 4-h test in the D4 batch was 20 mg/L 
as compared with 15 mg/L in the D5 batch, with identical pHs of 7.3. 
Thus, the expected ratio of oxidation rate in the test digester to the 
control digester is 81 %, very close to the observed 82 %. Thus, 
notwithstanding the stoichiometric oxygen limitations, the slightly 
lower aerobic sulfide removal rate in the test digester compared to the 
control suggests that sulfides were chemically oxidized rather biologi­
cally oxidized.
The contribution of liquid phase sulfur oxidation to the overall H2S 
removal will likely be very low due to the stripping of oxygen by the 
biogas production in the digester, however testing this in the offline 
batch test was not feasible. Comparing the immediate sulfide reduction 
in the control offline batch digester to the full-scale micro-aerated 
digester, which took approximately 30 days to show sulfide reduction, 
further indicates that the relative contribution of microbial liquid phase 
desulfurization was minimal in the batch tests.
The average biogas RT in the headspace of the full-scale test digester 
was approximately 16 minutes. Based on the first-order rate of 0.52 h−1, 
derived from pilot and full-scale studies with headspace micro-aeration 
by Muller et al. (2022), the biogas RT of 16 minutes would correspond to 
an estimated concentration-based removal efficiency of 13 %, matching 
the observed 13 %.
Typically, upper limits of H2S concentrations for biogas utilization 
vary depending on biogas use with limits varying from < 100 ppmv for 
combined heat and power engines (CHP) and < 4 ppmv for natural gas 
upgrade (Choudhury et al., 2019). Thus, based on the observed 2100 
ppmv without micro-aeration in this study, and the aforementioned rate 
constant of 0.52 h−1, the required biogas residence times would be 5.8 
and 12.0 hours for CHP and natural gas upgrade, respectively. Thus, in 
anaerobic digesters with limited headspace and/or floating covers bio­
logical desulfurization of biogas in the headspace is insufficient to meet 
the requirements, and therefore dedicated scrubbers, bioscrubbers, ad­
sorbers, and other clean-up technologies are required downstream. 
Although the biofilm surface area in the headspace can be increased by 
the addition of carrier media, such measures are unlikely to improve 
performance by the factor of 20–50 needed for necessary biogas quality 
upgrade.

the full-scale digesters subjected to micro-aeration.
The offline batch testing revealed several limitations that must be 
addressed. The stripping of the H2S by biogas production in continuous- 
flow digesters will decrease the dissolved H2S and slow the rate of both 
chemical and biological oxidation of sulfides in the liquid phase, despite 
being advantageous to biotreatment in the headspace. To simulate the 
conditions in the digester, with respect to both the generation of dis­
solved sulfides and their stripping by the produced biogas, the batch 
tests should involve addition of the feed sludge, as a control. Due to 
differences in oxygen transfer efficiencies between the full-scale digester 
and the offline batch digester, air injection rates must be carefully 
determined to ensure that the same redox potential, not the same 
volumetric air-to-biogas flows is maintained as the full-scale. Main­
taining the same redox potential ensures that the chemical oxidation of 
sulfides by various species is properly simulated in the offline test. The 
presence of even trace concentrations of iron in the digestate may bind 
with sulfides interfering the results and thus, total and dissolved iron 
species need to be monitored during the test. Offline tests should be 
done, using both the digestate and biofilms attached on digester walls. 
While this might be easy for bench-scale laboratory digesters, obtaining 
biofilms from full-scale facilities may be challenging.

4. Conclusions
This work demonstrated the feasibility of using micro-aeration for 
biogas desulfurization in digesters with very limited headspace by 
injecting air into the liquid phase as opposed to the digester headspace, 
achieving, about 13 % reduction at a biogas residence time of only 
16 minutes. In digesters with limited headspace, although micro- 
aeration cannot achieve the low H2S for biogas utilization in CHP and 
natural gas upgrade, it can be readily applied to reduce loadings to 
downstream desulfurization systems economically. Micro-aeration was 
beneficial for hydrolysis, as evidenced by the higher soluble COD in the 
test digester.
Offline batch testing indicated that in the absence of biogas pro­
duction, the kinetics of dissolved sulfides reduction with N2, air, and 
H2O2 followed zero-order, with rate constants varying from 0.029 to 
0.056 mg/L-min, with chemical oxidation as the primary removal 
mechanism and no major contribution of SOM to dissolved sulfides 
reduction. The applicability of the empirical first-order H2S removal rate 
of 0.52 d−1, developed by Muller et al. (2022) based on full-scale and 
pilot-scale headspace micro-aeration, was evidenced by the identical 
theoretical and experimental H2S reduction efficiencies of 13 %.
Future research should focus on the optimization of micro-aeration 
in limited headspace digesters by the addition of biofilm carrier media 
in the headspace, evaluation of headspace kinetics particularly at low 
H2S concentrations that may restrict biofilm growth due to diffusional 
limitations, and delineation of appropriate scaling criteria. The deter­
mination of the kinetics of dissolved sulfide oxidizing bacteria in the lab, 
under oxygen-limited conditions similar to full-scale digesters remains a 
significant challenge, complicated not only by the chemistry of sulfide 
precipitation, but also by the need to emulate the same mass transfer 
conditions of the full-scale digester. Insight into the correlation between 
the relative abundances of various sulfur oxidizing bacteria and bio­
logical sulfur oxidation is lacking.
